questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$  

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-1) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. Any $5\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

II. Any $3\times 5$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

III. The singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ are negative.
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Since $A$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 5}\times {A}_{5\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. Since $A$ is a $3\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 3$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 3}\times {A}_{3\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )((5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$
